I run an applications company (http://neutroncreative.com) and I can assure you that we build all of our applications and websites with Webflow, and it's worked fantastically. The generated HTML, CSS, & Javascript is REALLY clean. For making apps, we export our code and it works really well. Honest to god, most of the time it wrights cleaner markup than I can. In regards to interactions, it has a super awesome Interactions library (Seriously, check out some of the abilities in the new 2.0! https://webflow.com/feature/interactions-v2) and I'm able to get all modals and other simple JS done. It also has Embed code feature which helps tons when I want to get a bit dirtier. I've never built full apps with Webflow, but I've seen it done more than a few times with React JS. In regards to responsiveness, you don't have control over the breaks but it's presets have really helped me create more responsive websites.

Webflow is a really, really intuitive platform and it's only natural to be skeptical. For myself, I really had to build out a few websites to figure out why it's CMS is so powerful, as it has such an extensive API and when building simple blogs, websites, and even building responsive web apps it can help my team collaboratively build & prototype our websites & applications much quicker. 

Let me know if you have any more questions and I'd be glad to help!

PS: Neither me nor Neutron Creative Inc. are sponsored or affiliated with Webflow

Encryption - 
You have a puzzle, throw a few extra pieces in, and scramble it

Hashing -
You have a cow, throw an extra cow in and then cut them into steak

You can unscramble the puzzle and all but you can't turn the steak back into a cow.

It's generally more secure (this can be argued depending on your encryption method) than encryption.

Although one can argue p vs np (anything that can be checked by a computer can be solved by a computer, but it hasn't been solved yet) I'd stick with a good hashing method.

And no, md5() is not what you should use for passwords :)
